projects.name: CI Kit
projects.tagline: Run your CI on your laptop, before you push.
projects.shortDescription: A local gate that runs the same scripts your GitHub Actions workflow runs, so the answer to 'did I break something?' never depends on a runner being available.
projects.description: CI Kit gives a repository a local gate that mirrors what the GitHub Actions workflows do: the same installs, the same linters, the same type checks, the same tests. It also runs the workflow files themselves locally through act, so the YAML can be checked without waiting for a runner. The design principle is a single copy of the setup: the gate scripts live in the repository under scripts/ci/, and both the Makefile and the workflow call them. There is one copy of the setup, so it cannot disagree with itself. The tool works with any language — the gates are driven by what the repository actually contains — and it deliberately does not take over your pipeline. The workflows stay the source of truth; the kit makes them cheap to try.
pillars: Runs the workflow locally via act

keyOutcomes.title: A feedback guarantee that a billing decision cannot switch off
keyOutcomes.body: On 21 October 2026 the largest repository in the workspace had 28 failing runs out of the last 30, none of which failed on code — GitHub had refused to start the jobs because of a spending limit. Every run failed in about six seconds. The local gate answers the same question in about a hundred seconds, and it says why.

keyOutcomes.title: Three real defects found in under four minutes, without a runner
keyOutcomes.body: A stale secret-scan allowlist entry that was failing the CI scan on a tracked documentation file, ninety-three dependency advisories of which eight were critical, and build artefacts tripping a working-tree secret scan. The first two were masked because CI was red for a completely different reason, and nobody could tell the two apart.

keyOutcomes.title: The claim is deliberately narrower than the marketing would be
keyOutcomes.body: The evidence document has a section titled 'What is not claimed'. It states plainly that the local gate is not faster than a runner, that no runner-minute savings are claimed, and that the numbers come from one machine and one workspace. The value of the tool is a guarantee of feedback, not a speedup — and the documentation says so before anyone asks.

projects.name: api-mock-services
projects.shortDescription: One process, zero dependencies, and eighteen mocks for the payment gateways, identity checks and messaging providers your product talks to — running in the test, not beside it.
projects.description: Every project that talks to a payment gateway, an email provider, an accounting service, a DNS provider, a messaging service or an identity check needs something to talk to in a test. This is that something: one implementation, shared, instead of a copy in every repository. There are no dependencies. The mocks are built on Node's own HTTP server, so they run in a test, in a container and on a laptop without being installed first. The rules that keep it light are not preferences — a contributor who breaks one of them breaks the promise in the first line of the README — and the footprint is enforced as a build gate, so the promise is checked on every build rather than asserted in a paragraph.
pillars: In the test, not beside it

keyOutcomes.title: A fifth of the memory and a fraction of the idle CPU
keyOutcomes.body: Measured on the same machine with every mock running: one process at 50–51 MB and 0–0.5% idle CPU, against four processes at 250 MB and 7.9% idle CPU — almost all of it an OpenAPI proxy that also never settles. The engine that answers the first request in 0.4–1.4 s replaces one that took 20 s and was still rising. The ranges are the real figures: the script that produces them reports a different number on a busier machine, and both documents now say so rather than quoting a sample that happened to be true once.

keyOutcomes.title: Eighteen providers, including the African payment and identity rails
keyOutcomes.body: Stripe, Paystack, Interswitch, Flutterwave and Monnify for payments. YouVerify, Smile ID and IdentityPass for identity. Twilio, Termii, OneSignal, WhatsApp and FCM for messaging. Resend, Xero, Cloudflare, OpenAI and S3 for everything else. Every mock answers /health, so a container can be checked without knowing which mock it is.

keyOutcomes.title: The promise is a build gate, not a paragraph
keyOutcomes.body: The footprint test fails the build if the engine exceeds 100 MB, 5 seconds of startup or 1% idle CPU. A promise nobody checks erodes. This one is checked on every build, which is why the numbers on this page can be stated without hedging.

projects.name: Automation Gateway
projects.tagline: Air-gapped workflow execution as declarative JSON, with an audit trail that stays on the host.
projects.shortDescription: A Windows Service orchestration engine that runs enterprise workflows from JSON blueprints — no internet, no cloud dependencies, and a transactional SQLite record of every step attempt.
projects.description: An air-gapped, zero-dependency automation platform built to run as a continuous background Windows Service. It decouples orchestration from business logic completely: multi-stage pipelines are declared as data-driven JSON blueprints and executed inside non-blocking background memory sandboxes, while the engine core stays immutable and composable. Nothing in the request path needs the internet, a cloud AI gateway, or a package manager — the platform ships as a folder, is registered as a service, and runs.
projects.status: In development — repository to be published

stats.label: Audit granularity
stats.detail: Retrying, Success and Failed written to SQLite

keyOutcomes.title: Business logic became reviewable data
keyOutcomes.body: A pipeline is a JSON blueprint that can be diffed, audited, replayed and approved. Adding a step no longer means a controller change and a deploy — which is the wrong tool for a business rule.

keyOutcomes.title: The engine core is never edited to add an integration
keyOutcomes.body: Dropping a *.plugin.ps1 file into the plugins directory is the whole extension procedure. The engine core is a separate module scope with a composition root, so a plugin cannot reach into it.

keyOutcomes.title: Every attempt is recorded, including the retries
keyOutcomes.body: A step that throws is retried with exponential backoff, and each attempt writes a distinct state row. An auditor can trace the transient failure, the recovery delay, and the final outcome without reconstructing anything from logs.

naming.note: The mock engine's repository, npm scope and package name are all api-mock-services. Earlier drafts referred to it as 'SaaS-LocalStack'. The site uses the real name so that every link resolves to a repository that exists — a reviewer who clicks through and finds a different project has been handed a reason to doubt the rest.
